question: Why is the decode phase of a small LLM usually limited by memory bandwidth on edge devices?

answers.answer: Each new token reprocesses the full prompt in one parallel pass, so the GPU core count sets the token rate.
answers.feedback: That describes prefill, which is compute-bound. Decode generates one token at a time.

answers.answer: Each new token needs a full pass over all model weights, so the bytes read from RAM per token set the token rate.
answers.feedback: Correct. Decode is a matrix-vector step per token, so every weight is streamed from memory each time.

answers.answer: Each new token is first sent to a remote tokenizer web service, so the network round-trip time sets the token rate.
answers.feedback: Tokenization runs locally, in microseconds, and needs no network.

answers.answer: Each new token triggers a fresh re-quantization of every weight, so the CPU clock speed sets the token rate.
answers.feedback: Weights are quantized once, ahead of time, when the GGUF or .pte file is created.

question: A 1B-parameter model is stored with 4-bit weights. About how much memory do the weights need?

answers.answer: About 2 GB: one billion weights at two bytes each, which matches the size of the original FP16 checkpoint.
answers.feedback: Two bytes per weight is FP16, not 4-bit.

answers.answer: About 4 GB: one billion weights at four bytes each, which matches the size of a full FP32 training copy.
answers.feedback: Four bytes per weight is FP32, not 4-bit.

answers.answer: About 0.5 GB: one billion weights at half a byte each, plus a small extra amount for the group scales.
answers.feedback: Correct. 4 bits = 0.5 bytes per weight; real Q4_K_M files are roughly 10-30 % larger because of scales and higher-precision embeddings.

answers.answer: About 1 GB: one billion weights at one byte each, which matches the size of an INT8 quantized checkpoint.
answers.feedback: One byte per weight is INT8, not 4-bit.

question: What does 'open-weight' mean for a language model such as Qwen2.5 or Llama 3.2?

answers.answer: The model is only reachable through a paid cloud API, but its system prompts are published for anyone to read.
answers.feedback: That is a closed, API-only model.

answers.answer: The full training data and training code are released, so that anyone can retrain the model from scratch.
answers.feedback: That describes a fully open-source model (e.g. OLMo). Open-weight models release the weights, not necessarily the data or code.

answers.answer: The model weights stay encrypted on the device and are unlocked by a licence key from the cloud provider.
answers.feedback: Open-weight files are plain downloadable checkpoints (e.g. safetensors or GGUF).

answers.answer: The trained weights can be downloaded and run locally, under a licence that may still restrict some uses.
answers.feedback: Correct. Always read the licence: Apache 2.0 and MIT are permissive; community licences (Llama, Gemma) add conditions.

question: Time To First Token (TTFT) is mostly determined by which stage of LLM inference?

answers.answer: Prefill: the whole prompt is processed in one parallel pass to build the KV cache before any output appears.
answers.feedback: Correct. Longer prompts mean a longer prefill, so TTFT grows with prompt length.

answers.answer: Decode: each output token is generated one at a time while every weight is read again from memory.
answers.feedback: Decode sets the tokens-per-second rate after the first token, not TTFT.

answers.answer: Detokenize: the generated token IDs are turned back into readable text before the reply is shown.
answers.feedback: Detokenizing is a fast lookup and adds almost nothing to TTFT.

answers.answer: Download: the model file is fetched again from the Hugging Face Hub each time that a new chat request arrives.
answers.feedback: The model is downloaded once and then loaded from local storage.

question: What does the KV cache store, and why does it matter on edge devices?

answers.answer: The quantization scales of each weight group, so weights can be decoded; it grows with the vocabulary size.
answers.feedback: Scales are part of the quantized weight file, not the KV cache.

answers.answer: The tokenizer vocabulary and merge rules, so text can be split into tokens; it grows with the language count.
answers.feedback: The tokenizer is a separate, fixed-size file.

answers.answer: The attention keys and values of earlier tokens, so they are not recomputed; it grows with context length.
answers.feedback: Correct. KV bytes = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes x tokens, so long contexts can need more RAM than the weights.

answers.answer: The sampled output tokens of earlier chat replies, so answers can be reused; it grows with the user count.
answers.feedback: Response caching is an application feature, not the KV cache.

question: Which file format and runtime pairing is used by llama.cpp and Ollama for local LLMs?

answers.answer: PTE files holding 8da4w weights made by ExecuTorch, run by XNNPACK delegate kernels on mobile CPUs.
answers.feedback: That is the ExecuTorch path (optional extension in this lab).

answers.answer: TFLite files holding INT8 weights made by LiteRT, run by the NNAPI delegate on Android smartphones.
answers.feedback: That is the TensorFlow Lite / LiteRT path used for many vision models.

answers.answer: ONNX files holding FP16 weights made by Optimum, run by the DirectML provider on Windows GPUs.
answers.feedback: That is an ONNX Runtime path.

answers.answer: GGUF files holding k-quant weights such as Q4_K_M, run by C/C++ kernels on CPU, CUDA or Metal.
answers.feedback: Correct. GGUF bundles quantized weights, tokenizer and metadata in one file for llama.cpp-based runtimes.

question: Why can a Mixture-of-Experts model such as Qwen3-30B-A3B still be hard to run on a phone, although only about 3B parameters are active per token?

answers.answer: All 30B parameters are still computed for every token, even though the model card advertises about 3B.
answers.feedback: Only the routed experts (about 3B parameters) are computed per token.

answers.answer: All 30B parameters must still be held in memory, even though each token computes with only about 3B.
answers.feedback: Correct. MoE cuts compute per token, but every expert must be resident, so RAM needs follow the total size.

answers.answer: All 30B parameters are re-downloaded on each request, because experts are streamed from the cloud.
answers.feedback: Local MoE models are downloaded once, like any other model.

answers.answer: All 30B parameters must stay in FP32 precision, because expert routing breaks with quantized weights.
answers.feedback: MoE models are routinely quantized, e.g. to Q4_K_M GGUF.

question: Energy per generated token is best estimated from which measurements?

answers.answer: Model parameter count multiplied by the context length, which gives the joules per token on that device.
answers.feedback: Neither quantity is a unit of power or time.

answers.answer: Peak TOPS rating divided by the model file size in bytes, which then gives the joules per token on that device.
answers.feedback: TOPS is a peak compute rating, not a power measurement.

answers.answer: Tokenizer vocabulary size divided by the batch size used, which gives the joules per token on that device.
answers.feedback: Vocabulary and batch size do not measure energy.

answers.answer: Device power draw in watts multiplied by seconds per token, which gives the joules per token on that device.
answers.feedback: Correct. Joules = watts x seconds; scale to kWh per 1M tokens and multiply by the grid factor (e.g. 0.5562 kg CO2e/kWh for Thailand) for carbon.

question: When a very small model (under 1B parameters) is quantized to 4 bits, what is the main risk?

answers.answer: Answer quality can drop noticeably, because small models have less redundancy to absorb the rounding error.
answers.feedback: Correct. Compare Q8_0 and Q4_K_M outputs in Section 6.7; small models often justify 6-8 bit weights.

answers.answer: Token speed can drop noticeably, because the 4-bit weights are expanded to FP32 before every matrix multiply.
answers.feedback: Kernels dequantize in small tiles on the fly; 4-bit decoding is normally faster because fewer bytes are read.

answers.answer: File size can grow noticeably, because 4-bit formats keep a full FP16 copy of the weights as a fallback.
answers.feedback: GGUF quantized files do not keep a full-precision copy.

answers.answer: Context length can drop noticeably, because 4-bit weights cap the KV cache at a maximum of 512 tokens.
answers.feedback: Weight precision does not cap the context length; the KV cache is sized separately.

question: Why might the Edge_AI_Perf ratio estimate be optimistic for a Raspberry Pi 5 running an LLM?

answers.answer: It scales by memory bandwidth ratios, but LLM decoding is mostly limited by peak compute (TOPS / TFLOPS).
answers.feedback: This is the reverse of the real limitation.

answers.answer: It scales by thermal design power ratios, but LLM decoding is mostly limited by the SD card read speed.
answers.feedback: Weights are loaded into RAM once; storage speed affects load time, not decoding.

answers.answer: It scales by peak compute (TOPS / TFLOPS) ratios, but LLM decoding is mostly limited by memory bandwidth.
answers.feedback: Correct. The library does not yet model memory speed, so compare it with the bandwidth ceiling from Section 6.5.

answers.answer: It scales by the unit cost of each device, but LLM decoding is mostly limited by the operating system used.
answers.feedback: The library uses peak compute ratios, not price.
